params.text:
Raising and reporting a concern

If you suspect abuse or neglect, act promptly. First make sure the person is safe and, if someone is in immediate danger or a crime is happening, call 999. If someone needs urgent medical help, get it. Then follow the safeguarding steps below.

  • Preserve evidence — do not clean up, move or tidy anything that might be needed later, and avoid asking leading questions.
  • Record the facts — write down what you saw or were told as soon as possible, using the person's own words where you can, with the date, time and your name. Keep opinion separate from fact, and sign and date your notes.
  • Report without delay — tell your manager or your organisation's safeguarding lead, following your local safeguarding policy and its timescales.

Your provider must then raise the concern with the local authority, which is the lead agency for safeguarding enquiries under the Care Act. If the concern is about your own manager, or you feel it is not being acted on, you can raise it directly with the local authority yourself. Clear, factual records help agencies build an accurate picture and protect the person.

Multi-agency working

Safeguarding adults is a shared responsibility, and no single organisation holds all the answers. Several partners work together, each with a distinct role.

  • The local authority — leads adult safeguarding and decides whether a formal enquiry is needed.
  • The police — investigate where a crime may have been committed.
  • The CQC — regulates care services and acts on concerns about the quality and safety of care.
  • Safeguarding Adults Boards — bring partners together to agree how agencies protect adults locally and to learn from serious cases.

params.alt: A care worker looking concerned, beside the heading “Raising and reporting a concern”. Key points: Preserve evidence; Record the facts; Report without delay.

params.question: A person you support quietly tells you a colleague has been rough with them but begs you not to tell anyone. What should you do?

answers.text: Reassure them, explain you have a duty to report it to keep them safe, and pass the concern to your safeguarding lead.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. You must never promise secrecy. Be honest that you have to report, record the disclosure, and raise it promptly.

answers.text: Promise to keep it secret so they keep trusting you.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. You cannot promise confidentiality when someone may be at risk. It would leave the person unprotected.

answers.text: Handle it quietly by having a word with the colleague yourself.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. It is not your role to investigate or confront. This could increase risk and disrupt a proper enquiry.

answers.text: Ignore it, as it is one person's word against another.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Every disclosure must be taken seriously and reported. It is not for you to weigh up whose account is true.

params.question: Which organisation has the lead role in adult safeguarding and decides whether a formal enquiry should take place?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Under the Care Act 2014 the local authority leads adult safeguarding and decides whether an enquiry is needed.
Incorrect. The police lead on criminal investigations, but the local authority leads the safeguarding response overall.
Incorrect. The CQC regulates services, but it is not the lead agency for individual safeguarding enquiries.
Incorrect. Your organisation must report and cooperate, but the local authority holds the lead safeguarding role.
